speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speechtext:
I desire to answer
a question that was asked last night just prior to adjournment by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), concerning the treaty that was signed at Washington on March 2. This treaty is for the preservation of the halibut fisheries in northern Pacific waters, including Behring sea. It provides for a close season from November 16 of each year to February 15 following, both dates inclusive. It provides for certain dispositions to enforce that restriction. It provides also for the appointment of a commission composed of two members from each country, to investigate the life history of halibut and to make a report to both governments as to the best means of preserving those important fisheries. The treaty is for a term of five years, to be continued thereafter until two years after either party has notified the other that it wishes to put an end to the treaty. It will be printed in due time, but in the meantime I desire to lay on the Table of the House a typewritten copy of the treaty.
Who signed the treaty?

As
regards the negotiations in relation to this treaty, was there any change in the status of Canada in connection with the British Embassy at Washington?

I will answer the question of my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) and perhaps the hon. member (Mr. Maclean) will draw his own conclusions. The

treaty was signed by the United States of America, Mr. Charles Evan Hughes, Secretary of State for the United States, acting as plenipotentiary for the President; and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries of Canada, acting as plenipotentiary for His Majesty the King.

I understand that neither the name of the British Ambassador nor that of anyone representing Great Britain appears in the treaty, nor was any representative of the British government consulted as to its negotiation.
The treaty is signed by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, having full authority from His Majesty the King, to sign it as his plenipotentiary.

Is there any
change in the status?
Were the contents made known in any way to the British government prior to the execution of the treaty?
Yes, certainly.
Then my hon. friend agrees that there is no change in the procedure.
Well, my right hon. friend may draw his own conclusions.
I certainly will draw mine, but I was asking the minister what his were.

This treaty will be considered by a committee of the House and by the House itself, and when that is done I think it will be ample time to discuss the merits of the treaty and even the phase of the subject raised by my right hon. friend.
I have another question to ask regarding the subject. Will my hon. friend tell us upon what decision of this parliament the treaty was negotiated?

The treaty provides for certain dispositions which were recommended in 1918 by the International Commission appointed by both governments-by the government of which my right hon. friend was leader and by the government of the United States. Among man}' other recommendations, a treaty had been prepared at the time in regard to the salmon fisheries of the Fraser river, and it was signed but was never ratified by the American Senate. Another treaty had been prepared but was not signed, and one of its dispositions was the very one which is now agreed to in the present treaty. That treaty, I say, was never signed; but it has been

unanimously recognized by the experts of the Departments of Marine and Fisheries of both' countries that it was highly desirable to enforce the close season, to say nothing of the other dispositions which had been recommended by the International Commission. I may say also that this disposition has been recommended unanimously by the members of the parliamentary committee which was appointed last session to investigate the subject of the fisheries in British Columbia. As to the question which my right hon. friend raises, I do not know of any treaty which was discussed in parliament before being negotiated. The discussion always takes place afterwards.

I am afraid I cannot agree with the hon. minister. I should like the minister, before he comes to the discussion of the bill itself, to be good enough to look up some of his own speeches and those of his leaders on the subject of secret diplomacy
I do not like to read my own speeches; I enjoy much more the reading of my right hon. friend's.

How many men were at the annual camp at Carling Heights-a thousand? -two hundred and fifty? Jt was a very small camp.
I will have to get those figures for my hon.. friend.
I would like similar figures for Aldershot and Camp Sussex, I understand there were very few men at either place.

The comment that one hears in regard to the annual drill as performed in Canada last year is that the million dollars which parliament appropriated for that purpose was very largely wasted. Very little drill has been performed. The camps are hardly recognizable compared with the camps that were held in years gone by. A system has been established, and perhaps a good one too, of drilling volunteer units at their local headquarters. Instead of turning them out to annual camp they are permitted to do their annual drill periodically throughout the whole year. That no doubt is a good system. But wherever I have been, and particularly in Ontario, the comment I hear on every hand is that the old time enthusiasm for militia service is, not gradually but rapidly, disappearing, and that little or no encouragement has been given to it by the government. There is no doubt, from the comment we hear in this House, that if the service were to be blotted out altogether a number of hon. members would applaud the proposal.
Hear, hear.
Now, that is not my view of the situation, and I am satisfied that it is not the view of the vast majority of the people of the Dominion.
You are mistaken.

But in regard to militia training we have started to go down hill, and during the past twelve months we have gone down so rapidly that it now becomes a question whether the expenditure of a million dollars of the people's money on such training as was given last year is not an absolute waste. There come times, even in the history of this peaceable land, when we call on the militia; in fact, only a few months ago this government had to call upon the militia in various parts of Canada and send them down to the Maritime provinces to preserve law and order. They were not able to get a sufficient military force in Nova Scotia; they came up to Montreal, to Kingston, to Toronto, to London, before they could get enough men to send to the Maritime provinces.

Does the hon. gentleman think that if training had been going on in the immediate vicinity of Sydney at the time of the strike, it would have been judicious for the government to send men from that training camp to the scene of the strike?
I do not see any reasoD why they should not do so.

WTould the hon. gentleman himself have done it?
Supply-Defence-Drill

The militia of Canada is essentially a loyal body of men who are in favour of the preservation of law and order. It has been for that purpose very largely that the militia of Canada has been maintained since Canada became a country. The minister to-day comes forward and asks for $50,000 more to continue his annual training. Last year his first proposal was to have $1,400,000 appropriated for this purpose, but a disturbance arose among his followers on the question and he moved a reduction of $400,000. The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) was himself active last session in endeavouring to bring about a reduction of the vote far below the million-dollar point, but-probably after a caucus or a conference of some kind with the minister-he yielded and the amount was allowed to stand at $1,000,000. For anything that is before the House to-day, and for all the training that took place in Canada last year, $1,000,000 should be ample. The minister has not, in my hearing at all events, justified his proposal to increase the amount this year by $50,000. It is apparent to anybody who goes about Ontario-I do not speak for other provinces-that there is a lack of enthusiasm among militiamen themselves in regard to military training and military organization; they feel that instead of being encouraged they have been discouraged by this government. That may be the will of this House of Commons, but in my judgment it is a great mistake. We should keep up an establishment at least equal to that which we maintained in pre-war days. In those days there was no charge in this country of militarism; I never heard it, if there was any. If we keep up the same establishment and give the same class of training as we did three, four or five years before the war, the military spirit will be maintained and the enthusiasm of the militia organization stimulated. But you have not that condition to-day; the manner in which the subject has been handled by the government and by this House has brought about a reduction of enthusiasm and a depreciation in the value of our military organization. We find ourselves, as we did last fall, in this pass: that where trouble of any kind is threatened, even on a minor scale, it becomes necessary to scour the country as far as London to get a handful of men to send to the East to quell a disturbance, or at least to keep the peace. If the old spirit existed; if the old militia units were organized and received proper training and encouragement, men would have been available in Nova Scotia or New Brunswick for all necessary purposes. Let us get back to the old basis of

training. The minister says he trains 33,000 men. That is a fair number, if the training amounted to anything. But the men come in in small driblets, a few at a time; they turn out at local headquarters and indulge, I suppose, in a good time for an hour or two and report it as drill. It is the best they can do. The men cannot be got; they cannot be induced to enlist in the various units; consequently the units are far below strength and both officers and men are discouraged. Unless the minister takes some steps to bring about changed conditions, the whole military spirit in the country is going to die out.

There is something in
what my hon. friend says; the amount now asked is smaller than the appropriation in prewar days. But ,1 would point out that we are asking for an amount which is within $109,000 oi the amount spent in the last year my hon. friend was in office. The reports from my officers indicate that the training last year was just as perfect as it was the year before. The cost of living may be going down a bit, and that may account for the decrease. I must take exception to my hon. friend's statement that the militia men are not enthusiastic; unless the officers all over Canada are deceiving me, the condition is very much the reverse. I visited a good many of the headquarters this year and I found great enthusiasm prevailing. The majority of the officers understand that we have to get back to pre-war conditions, that we have to cut down the expenditure in this connection as in connection with all other services; and I feel that in doing that I am serving the country and not neglecting any interest. My hon. friend referred to the fact that the department had to go to London and elsewhere to get troops for a certain occasion. The law provides that in a case of that kind you must take the permanent force. If we train a million men in the volunteer force they are not, under the act, to be called on, except for the time necessary to replace them by members of the permanent force. On that occasion we called on none of the volunteers; we strictly followed the act and called on members of the permanent force. If he were dealing with the numbers in the permanent force, my hon. friend's criticism might be applicable, but the act does not provide that the volunteer force shall be called out, except in an emergency, and even then it is to be replaced as rapidly as possible by the permanent force. Section 81 of the Militia Act, dealing with aid to the civil power, says:
The district officer commanding in any locality, if he is present in the locality and able to act, or if he is not so present, or from sickness or other cause is unable to act, the senior officer of the active militia

in any locality, not from sickness or other cause unable to act, shall call out the active militia, or such portion thereof as he considers necessary for the purpose of preventing or suppressing any such actual or anticipated riot or disturbance, when thereunto required in writing by the civil authority hereinafter designated in that behalf: Provided that so far as the permanent force is available, a sufficient number of the force is to be employed upon the duty of preventing or suppressing such actual or anticipated riot or disturbance before recourse is had to other militia corps, and shall replace such other militia corps if so called out upon duty so soon as and to the extent the permanent force shall thereafter become available.
So, as a matter of fact, the permanent force is the force that the department, under the act, is supposed to call on in such cases.

My hon. friend surely has not understood that from the section. It says, in substance, "Shall call out the active militia, to be replaced so far as available by the permanent force." Only to the extent that the permanent force exists is it to be called on. If there is not sufficient permanent force in the district, then the active militia is allowed to remain. The active militia is available there above and beyond the permanent force for the purpose of quelling a disturbance. It has been so used time and again.
I am not so informed by the officers of the department.
The law is there.

The law is quite plain.
If you have a permanent force available, you are to use it, but if it be not available, in other words if it be not in the district or close at hand, you can use the active militia until such time as you can replace it with the permanent force. That is as I read the act.

And to the extent the
permanent force is there. If it is not there to sufficient extent, you may use the active militia. This goes only to confirm the point made by my hon friend for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) that the active militia is available for these purposes. The permanent force referred to is the permanent force of the district; if not, why is the district officer commanding mentioned?

The district officer commanding is in that locality. The officers of the department, and the act bears them out, I submit, are my authority that we are to call out the permanent force if they are available. If they are available, it does not make any difference where they are available so long as we can get them, but if they are not immediately available, we can call out the active militia until such time as we can replace them with the permanent force.

Reference has been made here on two or three occasions to the occurrences last summer in the Maritime provinces, especially in Cape Breton. I think that in view of the panic that seemed to strike some people down there in the island of Cape Breton, some explanation is due the House and the country as to the circumstances under which the permanent force or that portion of the active militia, whichever it was that was called out, was called out. Why was there any necessity at all of having a large number of troops rushed into Cape Breton before there had been a single overt act of violence so far as I am informed-and I followed the newspapers pretty carefully at that time. Was there any panic on the part of the officials of the British Empire Steel Company? Did they ask for the militia, or who was it that was responsible for calling out these men? How many men were called out, and who is going to pay for them? I think all these are very pertinent questions, and I should like to hear something from the Prime Minister on this point as well as from the Minister of National Defence, because I remember last year when a discussion was going on in this House with respect to the Mounted Police, the Prime Minister expressed a very pointed opinion that only in the very greatest emergency should the active militia be called out to maintain the civil authority in Canada. There was so far as I am aware absolutely no excuse, no justification whatever, for calling out the permanent force in Cape Breton last summer. I believe it was an abuse of the powers given under the Militia Act.

I am not going to quarrel with my hon. friend about the Militia Act. I did not anticipate this matter coming up to-day, though it is perfectly in order, because I have to ask for a supplementary vote this present year to pay the expenses of the troops that were called out. When that item comes up I shall have all the information here, and if my hon. friend would let the discussion remain over until that time, it will be only a few days before we can have a thorough discussion of it.
I am quite agreeable.

Why was the 95th Regiment in my constituency of Digby-Annapolis, ordered out under canvas at Aldershot last summer and a few days later the order countermanded? I would also like the minister to favourably consider giving this regiment drill this summer.

I have not the details with me but I will venture the answer, and I think
Supply-Defence-Drill

it is probably the correct one. It is the custom in the department at an earlier date than the estimates get through the House to notify the units that are to train, but last year the estimates were cut down to such an extent that many units were unable to train. I think that is the answer. I shall be glad to give consideration to what my hon. friend suggests.

Would the minister tell us what proportion of the amount last year was expended on drill for infantry units, and then indicate the amount that was sent for drill purposes among artillery units, machine gun units and other branches of the service?
I can get that information for my hon. friend. The details I have here are not separated in that way.

I wanted the information for a specific purpose. I find myself in hearty accord with some of the remarks made by the hon. member for South Wellington. I do not agree with him, however, in his view that a larger amount of money should be expended for this particular purpose. I think that this money is largely wasted. In order to determine the value of this training I think you have to take into consideration the different branches of the service that are trained. As I recall pointing out last year, the value of this annual drill so far as infantry units are concerned is practically nil. I think it is of very little value. If you consider the training given you must necessarily come to the conclusion that so far as infantry training is concerned, it has two specific purposes. It is either training men for war purposes, or training them so that they will be able to cany out any functions they may be called upon to perform under the provisions of the Militia Act in aid of the civil power. That latter, fortunately, very seldom becomes the unpleasant duty of any militia unit in this country.
With regard to training men for war service, the important thing is the physical training. It is conceded, and was conceded last year, that it takes a period of six months to train a man for war. Now all the training any infantry unit needs for that service can be acquired certainly within a month. The great essential is to put the man in proper physical condition. That cannot be done in a matter of a week; it cannot be done in a matter of nine days; it cannot be done short of the six months required. It seems to me that under these circumstances the training for infantry units of the character which is car-
ried on is practically valueless. However, with regard to the machine gun and artillery units and other technical branches of the service, this annual training may have some special value.
Let hie indicate what happened last year, and I simply cite this to show that the training is not carried on economically. Last year artillery units were brought from the city of Vancouver for the purpose of firing a few rounds at Sarcee Camp in Calgary, a distance of 640 miles. Artillery units were brought from Saskatoon, and I think from Edmonton, for the purpose of discharging a few shots, and getting a certain amount of training, after which they went home again. That is not training men economically for these technical branches of the service. I am relying for my information on the newspaper reports, which I presume are correct. .1 see no reason why the man at Vancouver cannot take out the gun which he brings with him to Calgary, and fire a few rounds in some selected spot there, and the same with the man from Saskatoon. Why should it be necessary to bring these men at great expense over long distances, bringing their artillery equipment with them, and I have no doubt their shells also, just to spend a little time at the camp and then go back home to their usual vocations? It does appear to me, therefore, that it can be charged with truth that this training is not economically performed so far as the technical branches of the service are concerned, and that so far as the infantiy is concerned, the training is practically valueless. It is for that reason, Mr. Chairman, that I desire to know from the minister the amount of this vote which would, in the ordinary course, be expended for the special technical branches. It was my purpose to move that the balance be eliminated from the vote altogether.
I can give my hon. friend the figures in numbers of men as I did a few minutes ago. I gave him the number of artillery men-
I want the figures in terms of money.
I do not think I have that.
Could the minister state the amount approximately?

I will have to have a calculation made. As to the number of men in training the figures are: Infantry trained in camp, 8,851; men trained at local headquarters, including those trained in machine guns, 22,011; artillery trained at local head-

quarters, of which 2,329 attended firing practice in camp for 6 days, 3,038. That would hardly bear out what my hon. friend said that the artillery men were simply firing a few shots when they were in training for six days.
Of course they were not firing every day.
I suppose they were firing every day when the weather was favourable.

Before this item is voted I desire to offer a few remarks intended not for the committee alone but for the country as a whole. I am not of the same opinion as the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), the former Minister of Militia, who stated a few minutes ago that the present Minister of Defence should go further and spend more money for militia purposes. I do not agree with that hon. gentleman; I ask the Minister of Defence, in the interest of the people, to spend less money for this purpose.
It will be remembered that last session I expressed opposition to the vote then asked for of $1,400,000. The Minister of Defence had to suspend the consideration of his estimates for about two weeks and then was obliged to reduce the amount asked for. That action on his part was not satisfactory to me nor to many of the people of this country, but I thought that this year the minister would do better. Under the circumstances I am surprised that the minister is asking for such a large amount; it is altogether too much. It is all very well for volunteers in the cities to go in for drill and to receive pay for it; but I do not see why young men in the country districts should at great expense be carried from one part of the country to the other for a period of nine days. For what purpose is it? Really to have a little fun-that is what it amounts to-at the expense of the country. It is claimed that it takes six months' training, at least to fit a soldier to go on the firing line. Well, if the young men are only trained for six days a year-although I have not made up the calculation-it seems to me that it would take practically a century before they could become qualified soldiers. Therefore, I am opposed to such a scheme.
I am a man of peace, as you know, Mr. Chairman, I have always been a man of that type, and as I am getting older from year to year I shall continue in that frame of mind. It is hard for me to realize that all the members of this House are in favour of training our young men to engage in some future European war. Such an idea is repugnant to
the majority of our people, except perhaps the politicians. Is it not admitted by almost everybody that we have been virtually ruined as a result of our engaging in the last European war? I think we occupy to-day a very unenviable position, bearing as we do such an enormous burden in connection with our National Railways and having to support such an immense debt as a result of the
4 p.m. war. For my part I do not see how we are ever going to get out of these difficulties. Therefore, when men say, in this House and outside of it, that we should prepare ourselves for a future war I do not accept such advice, neither do the people of the country. It is altogether opposed to common sense, in view of our past experiences and present conditions, that anybody should suggest our going ahead and training men and spending more money for some war in the future. That is my point of view.
I know very well that the so-called big men in the militia want money voted from year to year for military purposes and for the training of the militia. They want to demonstrate to the people that they are doing something, otherwise they would lose their jobs.
Who are those men?

They are the brigadier-generals, the colonels, the majors and the officers of other ranks. Now the minister is asking for $50,000 more than we voted last year for annual drill, and $100,000 more for the cadet services. Will this expenditure be to the benefit of the country? I say, no. Whenever the need arises to maintain the peace in Canada we have to call upon the permanent force. If I am not mistaken the minister told the committee a moment ago that he had to despatch troops from the permanent force to Cape Breton when a disturbance occurred there. Why, I ask in the name of my electors, is it necessary to spend nearly $13,000,000 this year on the militia, the navy and the mounted police? After the recent war was brought to a close we were told that the last war had been fought, and that we were through with war forever. In spite of that we are still being called upon to vote these large expenditures for military purposes, at a time when the people are being taxed in so many different ways. Let me say, for example, that it will take a great many two-cent stamps to even begin to pay the $13,000,000 referred to. Do you not think, Mr. Chairman, that the time has arrived when this government should say: We are going to have a rest now in the matter of military expenditure; we are going to cut

I would gladly support some such amendment as that moved by my hon. friend (Mr. Lanctot), not because I want half that amount expended, but because this seems the only way possible to protest against the larger expenditure. As representing a Canadian constituency and a rather important one, I must protest against expenditures for military purposes. I think I may speak, not merely for one constituency, but for a large section of the labour people across this country from coast to coast, who almost unanimously protest against continued military expenditures. I notice that the items for militia, the naval service and the air force, amount to nearly $13,000,000. If we add to that the estimate for the mounted police force, which is more or less a military police force, although it is under another department, we have the enormous sum of over $15,000,000 which is being expended in this country for preparation for some future war or for some possible disturbance at home.
We ought to ask ourselves very definitely, as I said last yfear, against what enemy we are proposing to go. Are we proposing to keep down by military force any rebellion at home? What province in Canada is regarded as disloyal; what section of the community is regarded as disloyal, that we need to maintain a large military force in order to quell any possible rebellion? To-day we have had called to our attention the fact that the permanent force was used in the Cape Breton district during the past summer. I wonder whether that was a wise movement or not. I happened to be down there a few months after the occurrence, and not merely the labour people who were immediately involved, but business men, editors and others in that district were unanimously of opinion, as far as

I was able to gather, that this was a very unwise move. I wonder if the committee is aware that the military were sent down there in spite of protests of mayors of the towns involved. Is the committee aware that a force of some 1,500 returned men lined up in opposition to the military, and it was only the restraint, alike of the returned men and, I am glad to say, of the officers commanding the forces that were sent down, that prevented a fearful tragedy in that district? Was it wise that men from Ontario and Quebec should be sent down to Nova Scotia to try to subdue a number of the very best citizens of Scotch extraction, resident for several generations, of Canada? Surely, there are some other means of settling our industrial disputes in this country than by sending our militia from one province to quell a rebellion of Canadian people in another province.
Are we preparing against any other foe at the present time? I would like the government who are responsible for bringing in these estimates, to tell us whether they contemplate any action against the United States to the south of us-we with our eight or nine million people and over one hundred million on the other side. Could we make any defence there, if defence had to be made by means of military force? Are we proposing, as the last speaker said, to take part in any future European conflict? Whether or not members of the government or members of the committee know this, a vei-y considerable proportion of the people of Canada will not again stand for that kind of thing. It is all very well from time to time in this House to utter praises about loyalty to Empire and so on. Some of us claim to be as loyal Canadians and as loyal British subjects as there are anywhere; but we do not believe in some of the policies that have been pursued in the past in the name of the British Empire or in the name of the Canadian people, and the number of those who hold that opinion is rapidly growing. Are we preparing for any European conflict? We may well pause and ask ourselves such questions.
Probably we are going along simply on the old principle that preparedness is the best way to avoid war; that preparedness is a sort of insurance against war. That doctrine has been proved absolutely false by the events of the last few years. Preparedness carries with it no guarantee whatever of peace, and I take it that the big thing we have to learn these days is that the guarantees of peace do not consist of large armies, or of a large naval force or of an air force or anything of that kind. The guarantees of peace are altogether

different. We have been told by leading thinkers in nearly all countries that we have entered a new age. We have been warned that if we pursue the old methods, we are inevitably bound for catastrophe. I take it that we in Canada are at this time in a peculiarly favourable position to begin to work our way out into new methods for ensuring and perpetuating peace. We are on this North American continent side by side with a friendly nation to the south of us. We are eloseley united by ties of blood with Great Britain, France, and I am glad to think also, through a considerable part of our population in the West, with large numbers of European peoples. We have no hereditary enemies; we have no enemy that stands at our gates. Under such circumstances, I should like to think that we would .cut down these expenditures and take our part in showing the world a better way. We should take care of the wrecks of the last war before we begin to train our boys for the next war.

Are the people generally anxious to maintain the enthusiasm which some hon. gentlemen in the House would like to see maintained for military things? It is no use our talking about disarmament or declaiming against great military establishments in Europe unless at home we begin to put our theories into practice. We have a far easier task in Canada than is the case in Europe. We have not the animosities and standing armies they have in Europe. We have not the old established systems nor the military caste that they have in Europe; It is easier for us to begin the task here. I will gladly support any motion looking towards a reduction of our military estimates with a view to eliminating them altogether just as soon as possible.

I wish to make some references to the remarks of the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). When he was discussing this matter he intimated that I was reflecting on the loyalty and honesty of the militia of Canada. I asked him a certain question, and I had a purpose in mind in asking that question. I expected to get an answer, but I did not get one. However, I wish to call his attention to the fact that I had no intention of attacking the militia of Canada, either the rural or the city battalions. I simply wished to find out whether he himself, would, as Minister of Militia make himself responsible for sending untrained troops to the scene of a riot. I am under the impression and I firmly believe I am right, that five, six or seven days' training at a rural camp does not fit a man for military duty. It has been said time and again in this House that it requires at least six months' training to make a soldier, and a man who is not perfectly disciplined is the last man to whom we should entrust the use of death-dealing weapons. We had some experience in the city of Quebec during what was called the conscription riots. At that time the government of the day sent down to Quebec thousands of untrained troops in order to quell the so-called riots which the newspapers had advertised all over the country. Troops were sent down to Quebec who had never handled a rifle, and some of them, I am sure, had never seen a rifle before. On the evening of the day when they disembarked, they were lined up in front of the Canadian Pacific railway station at Quebec, handed loaded Ross rifles, and sent out to keep peace and order in the good city of Quebec. The result, as every one knows, was that a large number of these men, already inflamed by the stories which they had read, and probably by some of the violent denunciations of the province of Quebec which they had heard from some of my hon. friends, were so excited that within a very short time when the first few snowballs were thrown at them they opened fire and a considerable number of people were wounded and some, unfortunately, killed. While the minister was giving us these details I added the amounts expended on six rural corps; they amounted approximately to $10,000. That, on a total of $58,000 for the particular district with which I am familiar, would be probably about one-fifth. So, if my hon. friend (Mr. Lanctot) would ask that this amount be reduced by one-fifth, I think he would be carrying out his own views and would probably meet with the approval of a large number of hon. members. I understand that very many hon. members opposite see no reason why there should be a distinction between rural and urban corps. There is this difference. There may be some reason for training urban troops; personally I do not see it, but I am told that there is. If there is, it is because these soldiers of the city are close to the scene of their operations; they can very easily repair every night to the local drill hall and carry on their training work; and they can meet outside the time allowed for drill, and so can cultivate esprit de corps-they can have a real militia organization of some kind. On the other hand the young men from country districts often live too far apart from one another to maintain any permanent organization of any sort. As a rule it takes them one day to get to camp and one day to return, and another day of the camp period is Sunday; so that they have but five or six days a year at most at camp, and the training given to them is, to my mind, utterly useless; it is of no value whatsoever.
Apart from that, I do not consider that at the present time we require any military camps, a matter upon which I have already expressed my views to this House. We have in Canada a sufficient number of trained troops for any eventuality which may arise. It is true that last year some hon. members
said that those who had taken part in the last war should not be forced to go to the next outbreak of hostilities. Great commiseration was expressed for those who had participated in the great struggle which began in 1914, and certain members were horrified to think that these veterans might be called upon to go to another war. But it will be remembered that during the course of last summer, when a little scare arose throughout the country, the first to volunteer for active service overseas were veterans of the last war, in fact the government was deluged with offers from them. Now, I stated last year, and I repeat-without fear of contradiction this time because the facts have borne me out- that in the event of another war breaking out in the near future, the first men to volunteer and the first men to go will be those who took part in the last great struggle. Taking that, for granted, and I think every hon. member must agree with me, we have in Canada three to four hundred thousand trained troops. And we do not need any more; in that number of trained men we have an ample force to protect us in case of any trouble arising. Let us, then, consider why we should have any training at all. I have already said that in my opinion we should not have any, but apparently I do not seem to be able to find a sufficient number of members here to support my views on this matter. However, I am prepared to go to the length of meeting the committee a little more than half way, and to ask the minister to reduce his estimates by the amount which he has included for the training of rural battalions.

I think if my hon. friend proposed to break up the militia that would be the easiest way to do it. It would be easy to say that in Canada we were going to make a distinction, as to the young men that we allow to join our militia or to have any training, between the cities and the country. That would be a mistake from the militia standpoint, I think. It may be true that in the sections named by my hon. friend the rural units do not train to such an extent as the city units do; but in many parts of this country the rural units are more enthusiastic than the city units are, and some of the best officers in the militia belong to rural units. I imagine that such a distinction as my hon. friend proposes to make could not be seriously entertained. Think of the effect it would have all over the country.
The hon. member (Mr. Power) has referred to the fact that many men who had
5 p.m. been overseas were enthusiastic in volunteering their services once more
Suppl y-D ejence-Drill

last summer. That is true, but is it fair, bearing in mind the sacrifices which they have made to take this stand? "You say you will go again. Hurrah! The rest of us will stay at home including the young men, who are just as anxious to go as those who have already served overseas." I am not a militarist or anything of the kind, but as I have already said, if there are to be wars we must have a militia. The Dominion of Canada unanimously agreed years ago to take over the militia from Great Britian. We have had a militia force ever since that time, and it is our duty to maintain such a force of reasonable proportions at an expense that will not be too great.
I have been asked whether these units could be trained for less expenditure. They might, but I think I should not be asked-and'if I were I could not consent-to make any distinction between the rural units and the city units so far as the expenditure of money for the training of our young men is concerned. This amount of $1,050,000 is less than it was n pre-war times, notwithstanding that the lost of maintaining the militia is at least from 50 to 75 per cent higher than it was then. Personally I could not recommend to the House that we should reduce this item at all. I believe the people of Canada will be with us in endeavouring to maintain a militia force of respectable proportions at as cheap a cost as such a force can be maintained for in this country.
Would the minister tell us what the effect of reducing last year's vote was?	[DOT]

The effect of the reduction last year was-I am not making a comparison with the year before because I think the training was practically as good as it was the year before, but with previous years-that a larger number of men were trained in that the units were more nearly up to strength than they were years ago. In other cases some of the units were not trained at all. I may say that the Chief of Staff, in order to give full military training, asked me for a vote of $1,750,000, but the amount was reduced, with his full consent on discussion with him, to the present vote of $1,050,000. I think this is a very moderate estimate of the amount required for training.

With reference to Military District No. 2, which is Toronto, I would like to know what proportion of the allotment of that district was devoted to the rural battalions and what proportion to the city battalions. So far as my knowledge goes, and

I realize it is very limited, the battalion in my own county went to camp about one-half strength. They were anxious to go stronger, but the money was not available.

What one was that?
Mr. BO\S: The 35th Simcoe Foresters. I want to join with the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) in putting in a word for the rural battalion. If we are to have drill, we must have it in the country just as much as in the city, and if the battalions are to be cut right down to one-half or one-third strength, I do not believe you will get satisfactory results. Before I cast a vote, I should like, if possible, to know what the ratio of expenditure was last year, and whether or not it is the intention to maintain that ratio for next year. If it is as low as has been suggested by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), namely about one-fifth, I would suggest that the amount that should be devoted to rural battalions should certainly be increased.

I think it is the intention of the Chief of Staff to spend a proportion of this $50,000 on rural units, as the city units have every facility for training at home. They can select their time of year for training and they do not have to leave their vocation to do any training. They can attend to their regular work in the day time and train at night. My idea-and I think this is the view of the Chief of Staff-is to increase the amount for the rural units rather than to reduce it.
I am glad to hear that. Can the minister give me the actual expenditure for the ten months gone by?

It must be borne in mind that in recent years the number of rural battalions is very much less than it was heretofore. Many battalions which were formerly rural have, in the last three or four years, become city battalions for the very purpose of allowing them to train at their local headquarters instead of going to camp. But there are some very valuable militia units yet which are rural battalions. The one referred to by the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Boys) is one of them; the York Rangers is another; the Huron Regiment is another. All of these, I have been informed, could have gone to camp last year, at almost full strength; but through lack of money for the purpose of drill or training, they were not permitted to go at full strength. There is not, however, to-day the same proportion between rural and city units that there was four years ago. The rural units have become

Supply-Defence-Drill
very much reduced in number, because so many of them have now; by their own desire, and at their own request, become city units.

While I do not wish to embarrass the minister in any way, I cannot refrain from making a few remarks on this most important subject. Probably there is not a member in this House or a man in this country who would use cold steel or cold lead more quickly than I would to put down any mob or rebellious crowd in Canada. By the cutting down of the estimates last year the minister won great credit throughout this country and great approval by the electors. There has been in the past an enormous waste by these annual drills, and this has been set forth very forcibly by the remarks of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) and the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw). Many years ago these annual drills were in the month of October, which was the season of the year when these drills did not interfere with agricultural work. But since these annual drills have been held in that beautiful month of June, when the crops grow fast and the weeds grow faster, when the bugs are trying to destroy our fruits and the vegetables of our land, it is a crime to call the farmer and his sons from the soil to go through these drills in the heat of the roasting sun.
Some hon. MEMBERS'. Oh, oh.

There is a good deal of laughter, but I want to tell hon. members who are laughing that this is no minor affair. If hon. members were called to drill in the scorching sun of June, they would see those soldiers blistered almost from head to foot. The officers have to call them off and to give them only a very few hours' drill a day, or some days no drill at all. I can assure hon. gentlemen that I am against this attempt to make soldiers, men to defend our country, by giving them a few days' drill at such great waste of our public money. It has been well said in this House to-day that we have some 400,000 soldiers who have returned from the great conflict, who will have discipline enough in their craniums to serve for a generation yet. We know that great conflict cost this country the appalling sum of about $2,000,000,000. We know that the taxation of this country is enormous. I come from a rural community and I know what the rural people think; I know what the boys and the men who go, think-they think this is a waste of public mono}7. I agree with what has been said as regards the large communities. There is where the pugnacious people, the warlike people and the strikers are. In the rural sections there are none of those warlike individuals, and I am sure you cannot take th* farmer and his sons and his horses away to quell riots at Winnipeg or Glace Bay or any large riotous community. I am in favour of a standing army large enough to quell the riots of these great centres. The great American republic have not had this annual drill. They have had a standing army quite sufficient to quiet any trouble in that great country. I would not object to voting money that is imperatively needed to keep soldiers who are trained, and well trained, to cope with any element that might rise against the state.
Let me tell some of the ridiculous things in connection with this waste of money on annual drill. Probably these estimates would go through fully as easily if the two ex-Ministers of Militia were less conspicuous in these debates. How attentive they were in their seats last year and how they beat the drum, and how they made it appear so imperatively needful for us to keep up the estimates or even give more! They thought that these estimates should all be increased. Let me say- and I presume there are scores of others in this House who know of the appalling waste of money-I will not use this locally-but there are certain grafters amongst captains^ majors, colonels, and those higher up. They go to the veterinary to help them and say: "Have you some old horses that look fairly well, that are about ready to die? Can you not buy up a few old plugs at $25 a head? You have been with us for many years and although you are crippled and no good, we would like to keep you. Get the best old nags you can	and	get	themthrough at $175 or	$200 a	head."
These horses are subjected to rough treatment and sometimes, being hitched by the feet they contract acute bronchitis! They are given such drastic medical treatment that in a short while they simply cease to exist. Then there is the chesty, stiff-necked fellow that buys the hay, and oats, and feed. If I were to tell all that I believe and know it would appal the committee. Although I was never a soldier, I have it from their mouths that this sort of thing was done to rob the country in pre-war days, and that being the case I can assure you that I am for cutting down the estimates. That nation is the happiest whose people do not engage in wars. Our sons and daughters are leaving this country to go to the peaceful land to the south of us, notwithstanding all that we are doing. I regret the fact, but I think we ought to devote some of the money to a real effort to retain our own people. Surely no enemies are threatening us. Certainly there are none to
Supply-Defence-Drill

the north, I am sure there are none to the south of us, and neither east nor west have we anything to fear. The Monroe doctrine would protect us from foreign invasion.
Hear, hear.

It is laughable and yet serious. Are we going back to the aboriginal age when the savages used war paint and devoted their time to the extermination of one another? Yet, when we spend all this money on war wherein do we differ from the savages? Have we no implicit confidence in our own people and our neighbours? Wherein is the difference between the mothers of this country who are proud to bear sons for a sacrifice in European wars and those mothers who cast their children into the Ganges or the Euphrates? Some people suspect that there is an enemy behind every post and pillar and under every woodpile and under everything that can conceal a possible enemy. It was with much regret I heard so many hon. gen-, tlemen advocating a year ago the expenditure of money for the furtherance of war enterprise. First, last and all the time I am a pacifist. But I am not enough of a pacifist not to fight to the last ditch if my personal rights or the national welfare be encroached upon. I do not wish to embarrass the minister, and while I might not go the length of voting for the amendment that is now before the committee, I do say that there should be less expenditure in this murderous, slaughterous game in which there are so many grafters and spendthrifts who are enriching themselves and wadding their own pockets. The civilized world is looking to disarmament, and I do not think that we should spend money in training our young men to take part in war. I do not think we should raise money-I was almost going to say, by extortion-from the pockets 'of the people when the farmers of the country are in such deplorable straits, when they have to pay such high taxation, such exorbitant prices for everything they get, and when they receive such unsatisfactory prices for the commodities they produce. If there is anything we can do, however small, towards paying off public debt we certainly should do it; and one way is to prevent the squandering of public moneys. Possibly anything I may say in the way of reducing the estimates will be futile, but undoubtedly in my opinion they should be reduced, especially in regard to something that only tends to build up a war machine for which there is no necessity. OUr population is not increasing and there' is no enemy in sight. And Heaven knows we do not want to mix up in European troubles, because those untold millions would absorb withfMr. Baldwin.]
out very much trouble the comparatively small number of young men we could equip. Let me conclude by hoping that the minister will not be influenced too much by the two exministers of militia who sit opposite.

What did the minister
mean by saying that we could not have a country without a militia?
No nation is properly equipped that has not a defence force.
Will the minister give me the information I asked for?

Fourteen units went into camp; the unit to which my hon. friend refers, which camped at Borden, being 160 strong.
Mr. BOY'S: What I want to know is the amount of money devoted to the rural and city battalions respectively, and the number of men who went from those battalions.
I shall get that information to-night.

I regret that my hon.
friend (Mr. Baldwin) did not say to what extent he wanted the item reduced.
Ten per cent.

In view of the attitude of some of my hon. friends I would amend my motion by substituting $210,000 for $525,000 or one-fifth of the estimates. That would be more reasonable and it would test the feeling of the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It has been called
to my attention that the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) has not voted.

Supply-Defence-Cadets

I beg to differ. I voted
against the amendment.
Cadet services, $450,000.

What is the reason for the
increase in this item?

I want it to be understood that I am more interested in this vote than perhaps in any other that may come before this committee. It is not true that the cadets are trained as soldiers, although part of the training may be of a military character. I maintain that the training given to these boys in their tender years is doing a wonderful work in building them up physically and making real men of them. I supported this vote enthusiastically for years when I was in opposition, and I have regretted on many occasions during the past twelve months that it was reduced last session. These boys in large numbers are given a summer outing with training that goes to make them real men in miniature. I have had some experience of the value of cadet training in my own family, and consequently I speak with some knowledge of the subject. Boys who are inclined to be weaklings, physically after going through the course of training for two or three years develop into fine young fellows and become straight physically, mentally and morally. I admit that I was humilated last year when the city of Toronto had to organize a tag day in order to provide the funds to give their boys cadet training. I helped the boys out in an indirect way by lending them whatever camping equipment they required. I am strongly in favour of this physical training for boys. It is given in the schools throughout our country. A boy can go through the course and be really made a man and yet never be a soldier at all, although I admit that a young fellow who is a graduate cadet makes the best military man you can get anywhere because he has the physique to start with. It has been said that this training is onlv taken advantage of in one or two provinces. The province of Quebec has a greater number of cadets than any other province, and this year they carried away the trophy.
And Three Rivers did it.
A small place called Three Rivers got this trophy-
Oh, oh.

-and I might go further and say that they did their training with rifles supplied by one, Bureau, and presented to them by himself personally. I will give the committee the enrolled strength of cadet corps at January 31st, 1923, by provinces:
Ontario: London, 6,841; Toronto, 16,976; Kingston, 6,836; Total, 30,653.
Quebec: Montreal, 32,214; Quebec, 13,432; Total, 45,646. Nova' Scotia, 4,329; New Brunswick, 1,587; Manitoba, 10,376; British Columbia, 5,838; Saskatchewan, 3,959; Alberta, 5,453. Total, 107,841.
These cadets are spread all over the whole Dominion. Last year we did not have enough money to give the boys their training camps, and I think we did an injustice to them from the physical standpoint. I am solely responsible for this additional $100,000, and I think the money cannot be spent in any better way than by training our young men and so improving them physically, mentally and morally.

Is this work undertaken in conjunction with the provincial Departments of Education, or is it under the direct supervision of the militia authorities? My contention is that the physical development of the boy is part of his education, and that it shpuld be fundamentally the duty and the privileges of the provincial Departments of Education to undertake this work. Therefore I should like to know if this work, with which I have a great deal of sympathy, is wholly detached from the Department of Defence as such, that is, as a military organization.

These cadet corps can be organized only with the full consent and approval of the educational authorities in each province. The Defence department, out of ' this vote, sends physical instructors wherever they are wanted, in order to give the training. Loans are made for rifle practice and so on.

I think all will agree that the young men and the young women should receive in our schools the best possible opportunity for physical development. A great many people, however, do object strongly to the effort made-shall I say?-to camouflage military training under the guise of physical training. As the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) has stated, physical training is carried on in every school in Alberta, the teachers being trained to give the best physical instruction to the children under their charge. Then, in addition, there are the cadet corps under the jurisdiction of the officers of the military district in which the school happens to be located, and this military training is earned on in addition to the physical training which is given in the schools.
I repeat that physical training is highly desirable, but I think it should be given as such, for that purpose and that purpose alone. May I, under this item, direct the attention of the minister to a resolution adopted by a com-
Supply-Defence-Cadets

mittee of students at the University of Toronto? It says:
Inasmuch as the Dominion of Canada is a member of the League of Nations which has been created to promote international co-operation and to achieve international peace and security, we, the students of the universities of Canada with a view to promoting the ideals of the league by bringing Canada into closer contact through intellectual co-operation with the nations of the world, and in the belief that only through the development of a mutual understanding between races and nations can war be eliminated as an agent of settling international disputes, go on record, through our representative organizations as in favour of the forwarding of a resolution to His Majesty'8 government of the Dominion of Canada, requesting:
That the government of the Dominion of Canada set aside annually a sum of money sufficient for the purpose of awarding scholarships to the countries and in the manner as hereinafter set forth:
1. TwenCy-two scholarships to be awarded to graduates of the universities of Canada for the purpose of pursuing post-graduate studies at any university in any country chosen by the students elected to these scholarships.
(a) The distribution of these scholarships as between universities to be based upon the enrolment of students in the universities of Canada.
(2)	Seventeen scholarships to be awarded among the members of the British Empire excluding Canada, not more than two scholarships to be awarded at any one time to any one British dominion or colony except that five be awarded annually to India and that two be awarded annually to native African students.
(3)	Sixty-five scholarships to be awarded on the following basis: South America 5; China 4; Japan 4: Russia 5; Korea 2; Hungary 2, Austria 2; Czechoslovakia 3; Spain 2; Italy 3; Bulgaria 2; Roumania 2: Turkey 2; Greece 2; Portugal 1; France 5; Germany 5; Holland 3; Denmark 3; Norway and Sweden 4; Finland 2; Poland 2.
The suggestion of this student body is that the government might take out of the moneys which otherwise would be devoted to militia purposes a sum sufficient to provide scholarships in order that Canadian students might go to some of these foreign lands and in order that students in foreign countries might come to Canada, the result being the promotion of a real spirit of international fellowship. I suggest that instead of promoting military affairs by the expenditure of vast sums of money at this particular time in our history, when these moneys are so urgently needed for other purposes, it would be advisable to consider the allocation of a substantial sum to meet the suggestion made in this resolution. I commend it to the minister as something that would make for that for which we are all striving-a better spirit and better fellowship among the nations.
How would these scholarships be awarded? Would it be done through the provinces, or through the various educational institutions?

The resolution outlines in detail the scheme which the students sug-
[Mr. Shaw.1
gest. They provide what is called an allocating board to allocate these scholarships.
Who would select the allocating board? When the federal government begins to interfere with educational matters, the thing becomes quite complicated.

Probably it would not be as difficult as it might appear. The resolution suggests:
That an allocating board be set up for the purpose of receiving the applications of those students elected to scholarships in Canada from their respective countries, for the purpose of allocating these students to the different universities in Canada according to course desired and the academic standing of the student.
It goes on to say that the board should consist of nine members, and there is reference to the manner in which its personnel is made up. There might be some difficulty in working out the details of the scheme. I simply present the suggestion made by these students as one which would be well worthy of the best consideration of the Minister of National Defence.

With most, if not all, of what the minister has said with regard to this vote I find myself in hearty accord. I would like however, to ask a question suggested by the stand taken by certain hon. members in connection with another vote, namely, that there should be a separate vote for rural and urban districts in matters such as these. I do not find myself in accord with that suggestion. I believe that all laws should be designed to give equal opportunities to all, so far as that is possible, and I am not at all in sympathy with any suggestion that there should be a different standard for rural and for urban residents. What I want to know is this: how far has it been found possible to extend the benefits of this training to the rural districts? I can understand that it might be more difficult to extend it to the rural districts than it would be to apply it to the urban centres, but I would like to know just how far it has been found possible to make its benefits available to the boys in the rural districts.

The benefit to be derived by the rural students would be this: the department has instructors who instruct the teachers. Last year there were I think, five thousand in line for instruction. These, in turn, instruct the cadets and can give the physical training in any school in the Dominion.

To what extent have the rural districts availed themselves of it?

Supply-Defence-Cadets

In forming separate cadet corps, perhaps not to a very great extent. But in many of these schools there are little companies of cadets, and owing to the training given by our officers the teachers are able to give the necessary instruction to both boys and girls.

In supporting this vote for the cadets-a work which, I am satisfied, is accomplishing a great amount of good- I would suggest to the minister for his consideration that it would be of great advantage to absorb some of the other boy movements that now exist in this country, more particularly the Boy Scouts. I think there is loss of energy and of organization between the Cadets and the Boy Scouts. I believe it would be very much to the advantage.of the Boy Scouts were they absorbed into the Cadets. It would increase the number of the Cadets very largely and would avoid the present division. I think that under the recognized discipline of the Defence department there would be considerable advantage to this country and to the Boy Scouts themselves by their absorption into the Cadets.

The trouble with the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. MacLaren) is that a boy can join the Boy Scouts when he is eight or ten years old, but he cannot become a Cadet until he is sixteen. I think you will find that in most towns the Boy Scouts ultimately join the Cadets when they are old enough.
In reply to the hon. member who spoke about the cadet movement in rural districts, I may say that the cadet movement is usually in connection with schools, and the children in rural schools-I am speaking more particularly of Nova Scotia-are mostly young; that is, if they want to go beyond a certain grade they have to go to the towns, and there they come in touch with the cadet movement. The physical drill is taught in both rural and urban schools. You could not very well have a cadet corps in the remote rural sections because there are not enough boys who are old enough to form a good cadet corps. I think it will be found, however, that the Boy Scouts generally do join the Cadets when they become old enough.

I think the age given by my hon. friend is hardly correct. The cadet age, I think, is from twelve to eighteen. You cannot merge the Boy'Scouts and the Cadets. I do not think that there is an effort made as my hon. friend (Mr. Shaw) suggested to camouflage militarism in the cadet movement.; and in proof of that let me give
just one illustration. Of the 6,800 Cadets in this district around Ottawa and Kingston, only 2,080 took rifle training, and that was voluntary on their part. There is no effort made to impose military training on them at all.

Are not these cadets trained
in all the military manoeuvres and in military drill?

Only so far as marching goes,
and that is not military drill in the sense of rifle shooting and so on. Physical drill is a part of military training, but has only lately been absorbed in the cadet movement as a result of the Great War that is done to harden a man. Physical training was a school preparation. I do not think any person connected with the cadet movement has camouflaged militarism, and when you consider that of the 6,800 Cadets in this district who took physical training, marching and such drilling as the teachers could give them, only 2,080 took rifle drill, I think you have the answer to that suggestion. I think that is worth bringing up.

With reference to the remark made by my hon. friend from Calgary West (Mr. Shaw) I would like to say a word. It was my privilege some time ago to attend the presentation of a trophy to a cadet corps. The general of the division, General Ami-, strong I think, was represented at that presentation. One of the speakers spoke from a military point of view, but the general's representative- said that the object of the training was first physical training, and then moral training. It was to teach the boys discipline, and he laid down this principle, and it is true I think, that a man cannot command if he does not first know how to obey, and the first thing a boy had to learn was to obey.
But apart from the physical training, the moral training I think is .very important. We talk about developing citizenship in this countiy. We know-I am talking to men of experience-that human nature is pretty selfish, and that if you were to boil down almost any kind of man, 95 per cent of the whole thing would be selfishness. That is the individuality of the man, and the idea of individuality is opposed to the idea of collectivity. Now in any well organized community what we want to do is to develop the idea of citizenship. I might be asked how I connect that up with the cadet movement. Well, as I was telling the boys in my town, "When you were training and marching and drilling, you never thought of Tom, Dick or
Supply-Defence-Cadets

Harry. You were thinking of the school you belong to. It was your Alma Mater you thought of, and you forgot yourself. When it came down to competing with the other, you thought about your corps, and not about yourself." That is the idea to develop in the child if you want him to grow into a good citizen. Teach him to forget himself a little bit and think of others. That is what makes a good citizen, to get rid of the selfishness, and think not so much of the individual good as of the collective good, and because of the moral results we get in this cadet movement I am wholly in favour of it. I think the minister is not doing too much. I think he did well to take it upon his own initiative to put this amount aside.
Physical training is also a very good thing. If you want to be a man, you want to be able to walk alone and defend yourself. That gives a man the idea that he is something, and when you get a boy to respect himself, he respects other people too, and respects property. No man has a right to ask his neighbour to respect him unless he first sets the example and respects himself, and I think this is a great school in which to teach the boys to be proud of their persons, and to learn respect for themselves, respect of other persons and of property. I think this vote ought to go through, and if all the other votes that come before us for consideration were the same as this, I would be happy to sanction them and to give them my support.
I would ask the minister who just spoke how he expects to train a boy to respect himself if he trains him to forget himself.

I have never preached in any church, Mr. Chairman, but I think that the greatest virtue of all is self-abnegation, and that is what I mean when I say that the boy is taught to forget himself. It may be that my English is defective, but if the hon. gentleman knows so much and cannot understand me I can tell him in French what 1 mean, in which language I can command all the words I require. If my hon. friend who is a former preacher cannot forgive a man for misusing a word in a language that he did not learn at his mother's knee, I can use French; I have enough of it.

I do not think there is
any necessity for the minister to get a little warm simply because I asked a question arising out of his own discussion. I was trying to get at the basis of this training of the boys. He tells us that first of all they are trained to forget themselves. I am not saving

that is a bad thing or a good thing. I merely wanted to get at the gentleman's philosophy. I want to make my protest, Mr. Chairman, against the passing of this item, and I quite realize it will only be a protest. I want to make it along the lines that have been laid down by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw) I believe that this movement constitutes a recruiting ground for the militia, that it is one of the means of instilling the spirit of war, the narrow spirit of nationalism, the spirit of conflict in the young generation. In short it is one way of instilling the spirit of militarism, the thing we have been trying to get away from. I repeat that it is a recruiting ground for the militia, although the minister tells us that the training given is not a training for soldiers. If it is not a training for soldiers, if that is not the fundamental purpose of this cadet movement, then why not allow this matter of training in physical form and so forth, to be given over to the public schools as suggested by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey)? We were told when the House was discussing the motion of the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) on race track betting that it was not the function of the government to moralize or demoralize the corfimunity. In that case why should the government take this matter up so strenuously ? If it is moral training you want it is not the business of the government, we understand, to do that. If physical training is desired that is not the business of the government either. If this is what the Minister of Defence (Mr. Graham) says it is, viz: not training for soldiers but training for mental and physical development, that belongs to other departments and can be done more efficiently by them. This government has no business to do anything along that line, and no appropriations for such purposes are in order under militia estimates.
I believe this vote may be successfully opposed on the ground of liberty. While our boys are not compelled to enter the cadet movement yet we are compelled to pay for the cost of the training, and there are great numbers of people who are very much opposed to this thing being thrust upon the community. In spite of that opposition they are not allowed to get rid of paying for it, they are compelled to nay their share of the cost. In

that way it is an interference with human liberty to compel taxation for that which is not sanctioned by the community. The community would vote the cadets down if they had an opportunity, and I would challenge the minister to submit this one question alone to the people of Canada through a referendum. It would not be carried; the people would not have it, they do not want it. We have other bodies doing the work of mental, moral and physical development. I wish to assure the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Graham) of my sympathy and support, and I do not think his position is a very enviable one when we are discussing the estimates of Militia or National Defence; but I am very glad to say that I feel in my heart that he is not afraid of the situation and that he is able to meet the arguments that are presented in favour of a decrease in our national defence. As regards the item that is before us, the minister is to be commended for increasing this amount for the development of the health of the youth of our country. I myself have had an opportunity for a number of years of being with the young men of my community and taking them out for two weeks' training. I feel assured that it is of great benefit to the boys in my community to undertake this training, this mental and'moral discipline. But there is one phase of the matter that I feel somewhat detracts from the movement, and that is this. I quite agree that it is advisable in the interests of the* health of our young people, that this cadet drill should have all the encouragement that it is possible to give it. I do not altogether agree with the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Irvine) who suggested that this parliament has nothing to do with the health
5G
of the people of this country. The health of the boys and the girls of a country is one of the greatest assets of that country, and nothing that can come before us at the present time is of more importance than the physical and mental well-being of our boys and girls. There is a great deal of good in this movement for which we are asked to vote the sum of $450,000. It will develop, not only what we believe to be the health of the boys, but also that which is so essential to national life- I like to call it the "gang spirit." In this movement, there is the spirit of emulation, the spirit of discipline, and when the Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Bureau), commenting upon this situation said "The boys are able to forget themselves," he spoke one of the noblest truths that enter into our modern civilisation. I do not altogether see the point of the statement of the hon. member for Calgary East that he did not see the connection between forgetting yourself and this movement. As far as I have been able to study philosophy, I think one of the greatest teachers said that the greatest freedom that a man could enjoy was when he forgot himself and when he willed the moral and social good of other people. The spirit of emulation and discipline which is found in the physical drill in the cadet service, is one of the finest things to help in making good men and good citizens. But there is one point that seems to find disfavour to a large extent with the people of our country, and that is the feeling somehow or another, whether it be right or not, that there is an attempt to introduce in this service the militaristic spirit that is prevalent. Personally, I am not at all afraid of the word "military" or "militaristic." I myself am the father of five boys, and if the time ever came when it was necessary for those boys to be called upon to defend their country, I should think that I had been lacking in my duty and that there had been something wrong in the training in the home if those boys did not respond. Yet at the same time I do not think this should be connected with what is called the cadet movement for physical training. It is the duty of the state to train men in a threefold way: physically, mentally and morally. This physical training, I believe, comes within the province of the state. But if in some way this federal government could cooperate with the provincial authorities, who have to a large extent the supervision of the education of the youth of the land, and if this government could assist them financially so that the boys and girls could receive the necessary physical instruction which is required
