to develop them, without fear of the suspicion that in some mysterious way the boys are being trained into soldiers, I do feel that the government w'ould have the approbation of all [DOT] the people of Canada. As matters are, however, it seems that this work must come under the Department of National Defence.
Now, as regards physical training under the direction of the provincial authorities, it is well known that every teacher is not qualified to give boys and girls physical instruction. In my own district there are men who are physically unfit to give proper commands and demand discipline; and in other ways it would be impossible for the average school to send its boys for two weeks' training on the camp ground. But if the Department of National Defence would limit its supervision to giving military instruction to the teachers, providing a course for them, or lending them tents or other necessary equipment, without in any way imparting a military taint to the assistance it gives, I believe the department would be doing one of the finest things for the boys in Canada to-day. I should be delighted if some measure could be conceived whereby the same privilege could be afforded the rural boys. I live in a rural constituency and when I come to Ottawa and see the boys in the public schools here getting physical training and the moral discipline that necessarily goes with it, it does seem to me that we in the rural parts of the country are handicapped. And that is why I am pleased to take thirty boys to camp two weeks every year. The member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw) submitted a proposal this afternoon which I feel that I could support, but not at the expense of this item. I think that the suggestion that comes from Toronto University is a good one, that we should have international scholarships by means of which educated people and ambitious boys and girls from various countries could meet us on a common plane and become acquainted with us, discussing our ideals of citizenship and our traditions, while we might learn something of their traditions and their outlook on life. That would be one way by which we could get into closer friendly relations and a better understanding with other nations; and to the extent that we understood them we should remove the fear of war. I should be quite willing to support the minister if he set aside a sum of money [DOT] for that good purpose; but I would not support it at the expense of the physical training of the youth of the land, for I believe that such training is one of the greatest assets we have in building up a virile citizenship.

Under our constitution the subject of education rests with the provincial governments, no matter whether it be physical, mental or moral education. How then does it come about that a vote which the minister justifies on the ground of education, and apparently on that ground alone, has come to be a matter for disposition by the federal government? I want to know the legal basis upon which this vote is asked?

If we adhered to the strict interpretation of the British North America Act, there are many activities which the federal government now engages in that could not be carried on. For instance, we are dealing with technical education federally.
That is perfectly clear; you are giving a grant for that purpose, which is to be used by the provincial governments in some particular manner.

We give the grant on a fifty-fifty basis. The federal government sent a commission of investigation all over the world where technical education was carried on to any extent to gather information on the subject; and a lot of money was spent for this purpose out of the technical education vote. The idea is that where possible the federal government should work in harmony with the provinces where it is thought that some mutual good can be accomplished. Take the question of agriculture. The federal government conducts a system of experimental farms. But strictly speaking, according to my hon. friend, that is really education,-agricultural education,-and the federal government should have nothing to do with it. On the contrary, we work in harmony with the provinces in that matter. They have agricultural schools and we conduct experimental farms all over the country giving agricultural education. Then there is the question of good roads: We join with the provinces in the construction of good roads. True, we give a grant, but it is subject to approval by our engineers; and we have a staff in connection with the Railway department looking after the construction of roads in the various provinces in order to ensure that they are up to standard. The housing scheme also might have been relegated to the provinces themselves from a technical point of view; but the federal government passed a vote and took a hand in the attempt to solve the problem. The simple fact is that w'e cannot draw too fine a line. The object of the government, I take it, is to develop the citizenship and resources of the whole Dominion; and the greatest of these resources is found, not in the bowels of the

Supply-Defence
earth, not in the timber, nor the lakes nor the streams of the country, but in the boys and girls who are growing up. And if, by avoiding rigid technicalities, we can join forces with the provinces for the development of all the resources that we possess I think we are doing a good work. Nor do I believe that we are violating the spirit and the real intent of the British North America Act.

There is in my judgment very much to commend itself to us in this vote. The work which is being undertaken by those who have charge of the cadets is an important, a desirable and a necessary one. But in my opinion it is unfortunate that it should be carried on under the auspices of the Department of National Defence,-unfortunate be-' cause that supervision seems to create a suspicion that the boys who are being trained are subjected to a militarizing process. While I am disposed to support the vote, it does seem to me that some attention ought to be given to the problem of shifting the supervision from the Department of National Defence to our educational authorities. In all the schools now we have physical instructors who are doing very necesary and good work; and I think it is highly desirable that this work should be linked up a little more elosely with our educational system, with the Boy Scout movement and things of that kind, as something separate and distinct from the activities of the Department of National Defence.

I said the law provided that if the permanent force was available it would have to be used; if it was not available and there was an emergency, the volunteer force should be called upon temporarily, but to be replaced by the permanent force.

That is what I intended to convey to the committee; perhaps I misstated the point. My view of it is that the Jaw does contemplate the calling out of the ordinary militia, the volunteer units, in the first instance. If language means anything, that is what the Militia Act of Canada provides. I just want to place the matter as it appears in the statute before the committee and let the committee judge for itself. This is a plain matter of fact and a plain matter of law. It will, I fancy, either now or hereafter have to be decided, and it is just as well that we consider it under this vote, which deals with the permanent force. Section 80 of the Militia Act is the law on the subject, it provides:
The active militia,-
That includes the volunteer forces of Canada as well as the permanent force.
-or any corps thereof, shall be liable to be called out, within or without the municipality in which such corps is raised or organized, for active service, with their arms and ammunition, in aid of the civil power, in any case in which a riot or disturbance of the peace requiring
such service occurs, or is, in the opinion of the civil authority hereinafter designated in that behalf, anticipated as likely to occur, and, in either case, beyond the powers of the civil authorities to suppress, or to prevent or deal with.
Now, the administration of civil and criminal law in this country is not left to the Dominion government; it rests with the provinces. A riot, a disturbance or breach of the peace, would constitute a breach of the criminal law of Canada, and it is the duty of the provinces, acting under the authority given them in the criminal law and under the constitution, to take cognizance of all such matters and deal with them. In other words, that is not the duty of this government or of this parliament; the province itself must take the responsibility and apply a remedy. The provinces have established municipal institutions; they have delegated provincial authority to the municipalities.

May I interrupt the hon. member? We had an unfortunate riot in Quebec in 1918. Why did the hon. gentleman, who was then a member of the Cabinet, not insist that the province of Quebec should take care of that riot?
Well, the circumstances were entirely different from those which prevailed in this instance. It was a time when Canada was actually at war and we had large military forces in the country, and it was-
Not openly at war with Quebec, was it?
No, no, not in Quebec.
Not openly.
The disturbance there was in connection with a matter with which this government had power to deal; I assume that is the distinction. However, I want to state my case, and if my hon. friend does not-
The mayor of Quebec did not call on the federal authorities.
No, the federal authorities# acted on their own initiative and should bear the cost. I fancy they did bear the cost.
They have not paid the victims yet.

My only desire is to lay the facts before the committee and let the committee judge. The municipalities maintain a system, in their police forces, for carrying out the law. If under any conditions the provincial system of police is not sufficient, then any municipality, acting through its head, may requisition the active militia of Canada in

aid of the civil power. If the head of the municipality refuses to take action, then power is given to the county judge having jurisdiction in that municipality. It comes back to the municipality, you see. The municipality is the one specially affected. It is to the head of the municipality that power is first given to request the calling out of the militia; then to the local judge having jurisdiction over the municipality where the disturbance arises. So it was in this case. I am informed that the head of the corporation involved and the municipality refused to take action. It was open then to any inhabitant to go to the judge, and on laying the case before him the judge could take action. Following up the provisions of the statute, he would make a requisition in the form given in the Militia Act, which would be forwarded to Ottawa, and upon that the government would act.
Now, how should they act? What I submit was the first thing the government should have done on receipt of that requisition was to call out the active militia in that particular district, in that municipality or at least in that locality.
How does the hon. member read that in the act?
I am going to read the act now.
I thought he had read it.
He is trying to edit it.

Section 81 provides:
The district officer commanding in any locality, if he is present in the locality and able to act, or if he is not so present, or from sickness or other cause is unable to act, the senior officer of the active militia in any locality, not from sickness or other cause unable to act, shall call out the active militia, or such portion thereof as he considers necessary for the purpose of preventing or suppressing any such actual or anticipated riot or disturbance, when thereunto required in writing by the civil authority hereinafter designated in that behalf: Provided that so far as the permanent force is available, a sufficient number of the force is to be employed upon the duty of preventing or suppressing such actual or anticipated riot or disturbance before recourse is had to other militia corps, and shall replace such other militia corps if so called out upon duty so soon as and to the extent the permanent force shall thereafter become available.
What I maintain in regard to that section is that the whole thing pertains to the locality. Any one reading that enactment which I have just read must come to the conclusion that it is the officer in the locality that can do it.
It is the officer commanding the district.
Let us look at the situation. The government had between five and six hundred men in that particular district at the time of the strike at Halifax. Were they called out, may I ask the minister?
Certainly, but there were not five or six hundred men whom you would call fighting men.
They were available men for the purpose. Then the next step was to call out the active militia of Canada in that locality.
Not in that locality.

Why, if my hon. friend's contention was correct, the two or three hundred men he could call out in that locality would not be sufficient. He would have to scour the country and go to Vancouver to get enough men to put down a disturbance. The thing is preposterous.
I did not say that at all.

As a matter of fact, he did not have to go to Vancouver, but he did go from Halifax to St. John, and from St. John to Quebec, and from Quebec to Montreal, and from Montreal to Kingston, and from Kingston to Toronto and London, and all that time there was apprehension of a riot or disturbance in Cape Breton. The meaning of the law to my mind is as plain as plain can be. The officer in the locality is the one you should make your appeal to. He calls out the permanent force in the locality.
It does not say so.

Then his recourse is to
the ordinary active militia of the locality, but instead of that the minister, under some authority which I suppose he obtained from the Minister of Justice, some opinion which he obtained from the law officers of the Crown, scoured the country from Halifax to London, Ontario, to secure a Jorce of men, at a cost of some $60,000, to go down to Nova Scotia to suppress this apprehended strike. Now what did it all amount to? I take the statement of my hon. friend from Cape Breton South (Mr. Kyjte) this afternoon, the government whip in this House. There had been some little outbreak, some little breach of the peace, a blow or two had been struck. Someone became afraid. The mayor of the city was not afraid. He knew that under the Militia Act, if the military forces of this country were brought down there at his request the municipality would have to pay the cost. That has been the law for a very long time and has been enforced in this

country. If a municipality seeks to have the militia called out in aid of the civil power, the law says that it shall pay the cost.

collected.

in many cases to collect a debt, but under the Militia Act, this becomes a debt due to the Crown. municipality to pay it? If the hon. member will look at the records he will find that he and his government attempted to collect very few, if any, of such accounts.

But this case I tried to
.explain as I went along. Now they could not get the mayor to act. He understood the responsibility. But the refusal of the mayor, if the judge acts, does not relieve the municipality. The judge can bind the municipality, if he is the judge in the district in which the municipality is situated, just as firmly as can the mayor. Someone went to a judge, and to a county judge having jurisdiction over the area. Personally I do not know who it was. My opinion is-it may be only rumour-that it was someone who had to do with the British Empire Steel Corporation. There was a strike on at their works and some difficulty had arisen there. They became afraid of what might happen, and someone went to
the judge and persuaded him that conditions were such that he should request that the active militia in Canada be called out. I assume that when the minister brings the papers down, we shall find out exactly who did go to the judge. But somebody went who had an interest in the matter, because the mayor of the municipality had refused to interfere. Then the minister sets about to gather up the permanent force in this country from as far west as London, and to bring them down to Nova Scotia to settle what looks on the face of it to be either a small breach of the peace, a small disturbance, or perhaps something that involved some danger to the company's property. My hon. friend from Cape Breton South this afternoon led me to believe that if steps were not taken to prevent disorder, it might result in the men abandoning the pumps and refusing to permit other men to work at them, and that damage might ensue to the company's property.
Assume that all is correct; I assume it is. Suppose damage did accrue to the company's property. The company has the same remedies as a private individual to recover that damage. If damage, through the wrongful act of somebody else, occurs to my property, or to the' property of any hon. member in this House, the law is there: We must take advantage of it and recover the damage. We cannot in every instance, although we apprehend that damage will be done to our property, call out the militia of Canada to stop it. I submit that if all they feared was damage to property they had no right to call out the militia at all. They had only right to call out the militia in aid of the civil power "where," in the language of the statute, "a riot or disturbance of the peace requiring such services occurs or is, in the opinion of the civil authority hereinbefore designated at that district, anticipated or likely to occur." A riot or breach of the peace either in being or likely to occur, is the sole reason for calling out the militia. Now the government called the militia out. They gathered up the permanent force from half way across Canada and sent it down to Nova Scotia at a cost to this country.-I will not say yet to this country-of sixty thousand dollars odd. In the first instance the Militia Act provides that that money shall be paid by the government, and that the government shall have the right to collect it from the municipality. The municipality which seeks the aid shall pay the cost. That is reasonable, that is proper, I submit. I understand the municipalities have protested that they did not requisition these troops; that they were not necessary; that order could quite easily have been maintained without them; indeed, that the disorder was due rather to the presence of the troops. I am not saying that they are right; but I say that if the government acted regularly, then the municipalities are liable, and the government can present to this House no excuse for not promptly assessing the municipalities in accordance with the law.
While I am on that point, let me emphasize this as well. I quite admit that if the requisition comes in the regular way and contains the proper assertions as provided in the act, it is the duty of the government, as is stated clearly in the act, to provide from the active

But the extent to which the government provides militia is not something that is fixed by the act at all; that is entirely under the responsibility of the government. The government is the judge of the necessity as regards the extent to which it shall send militia to take care of the situation. The government is not the judge as to whether militia should go or not. The warden, or if he fails, the judge, has that responsibility. The government gathers militia from the ends of this country right up into western Ontario, and sends them down to Nova Scotia at a cost to the country of some $60,000, a cost that under the act the country is never intended to pay. I know that it must be paid first of all out of consolidated revenue, and it might be very likely that a vote would have to be asked. propriety of amending the law so that the cost of sending those troops to Nova Scotia in this particular instance should not be assessed against the municipalities. The statute is archaic in that respect; it should be changed, and the expense should be borne by the nation. Of course, troops should not be called out without grave necessity. Perhaps the
power of requisition should be taken from the municipality, and I think it should in many cases. I would be the last to
deprecate any steps that are 'absolutely necessary in the interest of the preservation of law and order. Very good; the law is

If that were not the case, then the cost of the preservation of peace and order would be far greater than it is now, and the acceptability of the means of preserving it to the localities affected would be much less than it is to-day. Now, inasmuch as the responsibility is on the municipalities, on the various bodies constituted by the provinces, it cannot be in the power of the Dominion government to say whether or not these bodies are capable of carrying it out. House and an account of the achievements of the fleet? I noticed that on Christmas Day or New Year's he issued a message to the Canadian fleet at considerable length and of some rhetoric. Surely he can at least repeat that performance.

It is difficult for any of us but my right hon. friend to repeat a brilliant performance. The second time it is usually not quite so good as the first. I did not issue any classic to the navy or to the fleet. I issued the statement to the naval service. The act under which our naval activities are carried on in Canada is called the Naval Service Act, and it does not refer to the navy, but to the naval service.
It was on the advice of technical officers that a new idea in the development of the naval service was proposed and accepted by the House last year. Under that policy the cruiser Aurora, which I always maintained, and the technical officers agreed with me, was not a wonderful success as a training ship, was put out of commission and the staff paid off with the allowances provided by order in council. That cost in the neighbourhood of $70,000, if I remember correctly. The submarines were also retired. In place of the old policy another policy was announced during the last session. It was that the two destroyers would be retained, one on each coast, accompanied by two mine sweepers on each coast.
Trawlers.

I have learned that that is not the proper name to call them. They now have the dignity of mine sweepers. That is what they are for anyway. On the destroyers there are about 160 men all told. The mine sweepers will require about 25 men each, and the two on each coast are now being fitted out. One of the destroyers is now on the Pacific coast. So the fleet is divided into these two sections.
There are two lines of policy advocated by naval authorities. One is that it is the duty of a nation to prepare for high seas warfare, and the other is that its first duty is to develop the defence of its coast. There is a good deal of difference of opinion on this point among the authorities, but the technical officers in my department advise me that the latter is the proper thing for the Dominion of Canada, that is, training for the defence of our coasts. As the estimates only got through in the summer last year, we were not able to put the "Aurora" out of commission and pay off the officers and ratings until late in the fall.
Under the new system no training takes place except that carried on on the destroyers and among the permanent force. What is aimed at this year is this: The permanent force, officers and training staff, at Halifax and Es-quimalt comprises approximately 500 men. These are practically all Canadians, and that I think should be a matter of pride to the people of Canada. The policy I might say is based on the fact that the present minister, backed up by the government, believes that for this young nation the proper policy is to train our own young men for naval service so far as it is possible to do so.
In addition to that there are 500 men of the naval reserve. These men are professional sailors. They need no training in high seas service, but training in gunnery, and all that kind of thing, will be given them so many days each year at our training grounds either at Esquimalt or Halifax. Canada has a very large naval reserve in her men at sea. In addition to that the Navy League has done, and is doing, good work. The Navy League, with which we hope to work, has already placed something like 200 boys on Canadian ships, boys who have got their training through the efforts of that league. In addition to the 500 men of the naval reserve, we are providing for the training af approximately 1,000 men of what will be known as the Volunteer Naval Reserve. I may say that the first offer to raise a company under this programme came from the province of Quebec, from a brother of one who is already in the navy, but up till the present time no active steps, except preparations for the development and training of the volunteer reserve, have taken place. At Esquimalt and Halifax we are now busily engaged in the preparation of the accommodation which will be required, and we have purchased and placed at these points the gunnery equipment for training purposes. There will be a school teacher at Esquimalt and one at Halifax to train the young men that come in the rudimentary knowledge that is requisite for naval service.
In addition to what I have mentioned we have a number of young men being trained in the British navy, not officers but seamen. About 25 of these have recently returned for duty in our own naval sendee. Furthermore, young Canadians have been periodically sent over to be trained as officers in the British navy. I might mention two of these young men, one of them being the son of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Gauvreau) the other a son of Mr. Justice Brodeur. Both are very bright active young men and will make their mark in the navy. The object of
Supply-Defence

the whole navy scheme, as I have tried to point out, is not to begin to try to undertake the defence of the high seas-that is impossible for the Dominion of Canada at the present time-but believing that in years to come as we develop we will require naval protection, as we require a militia, it is thought best, at least by the members of the government, that the present is the time to give our young men that training which will fit them, both as officers and men, to take their place in the naval service of Canada as it develops.
Who is the present admiral of the fleet?

The present member for
Lunenburg (Mr. Duff).
There seems to be competition among the aspirants. However, I may tell my hon. friend the list of applications is not closed. At present the head of the naval service is Commander Hose.

Do these trawlers work
in co-operation with the British fleet?

They are mine sweepers
but my hon. friend insists on calling them trawlers.
Well, mine sweepers.

They did very effective
work on behalf of the British fleet during the late war.
I refer to the work of our mine sweepers at present.
There has been no war since we had our mine sweepers out.

I do not doubt at all that so long as we are protected on the high seas, so that >
nobody can get to our shores, the trawlers will be quite effective to protect them. My hon. friend calls them mine sweepers instead of trawlers, but as long as the high seas are safe at the expense of somebody else I do not think it makes very much difference by what name they are called. I am, though, interested in this programme of training 500 men-either 500 at Esquimalt and 500 at Halifax or 250 at each place, I am not sure which-and 500 more of a volunteer reserve, training them for service in vessels that do not exist and that the government does not contemplate shall exist. I would like to know what training they are to get and what they are to do when they are trained; how much training they get each year applicable to the force at Esquimalt and Halifax and to this volunteer reserve? These men are to be trained for how long each year-trained at 
what and trained for what? How long are they going to use their knowledge when they are trained, and how much of the expense is borne by the government and how much by private subscription through the Navy League?
And what will be their daily diet?

I hope I did not lead the House to believe that the Navy League was part of the organization. I may say that, with respect to the Navy League, the feeling is better than it was a couple of years ago. That seems evident from the correspondence we get and we hope to have some kind of working arrangement with them before very long.
I hope so too.

My right hon. friend has asked me a qustion about training. This is the arrangement:

Every year all ratings will be required to perform a certain number of days' training at one of the naval bases for which they will be fully paid.
The training will vary from 14 days to 21 days according to the class of rating.
All ratings will be allocated to the different branches on entry and will be required for that branch before the completion of their first period of enrolment.

After the 14 to 21 days' training, what authority has the minister for saying these young men will be trained to be of value for anything? Has he authority from anyone to say that they will serve in the British navy, because that is the only fleet in which they could serve unless they are going to serve in the fleet of some foreign country? Has he any authority to tell us they would be of value in the case of any emergency at all? In a word, is the training of these men of any value at all when we have no place to put them?

My hon. friend is pessimistic. This country is going to move. I have tried to point out to him that in the years to come as We develop and as we expand we shall, under this system, have young men of our own to put into naval positions instead of bringing men overseas to fill those positions. My right hon. friend forgets that this kind of training takes place in the naval reserve in Great Britain.

Over there they have a
fleet in which to put the men they train.

It takes place also in the United States. Wherever they have a reserve that kind of training takes place. Now

Supply-Defence
let me ask my right hon. friend a question: Is he in favour of militia training? If so let me ask him what good towards making a soldier does 21 days' training a year in the militia do?

The training for the
militia, as my hon. friend knows just as well as I do, is wholly different from the training for the navy. You can fit a man for service in the militia with a short training each year, although perhaps not under the system which my hon. friend provides for in the estimates he has brought down. However, that such can be done has been proved; but you cannot train men for the naval service with only a few days of service each 11 p.m. year. If my hon. friend proposes to train them for a few days each year, what is he going to do with them when they are trained? He has no place to put them. What career have they got to look forward to after having gone through this training unless they serve in the navy of some other country, or unless the government contemplates some indescribable naval service which does not exist to-day? If they are training men for a naval policy that the government does not contemplate, then this is nonsense. it is futile. If the government contemplates a different naval policy from what it has to-day, possibly this can be understood; but at present we are simply a laughing stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.

Just a laughing stock, just wasting money. We are depending on another country to keep our high seas safe, knowing no enemy wrill reach our shores, knowing that the only things that can reach our shore are wasps and hornets that could not give trouble even to an invader.
I am sorry my constituents are not present to hear the speech of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen).
There is one here.

While they voted against him at the last election, they would certainly go to the polls and justify their votes at the next election, because what he does not know about naval matters or matters pertaining to the sea would fill more than the seventeen pages which the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) lost out of his book. I think I am on record in this House as regards naval expenditure, and I am not here to-night to take back one word that I have said on a number of occasions in the different sessions that have preceded this one; but when the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) says
that he does not know what will become of those men when they have trained for ten or twelve days, he is quite right.
Does the hon. member know?

Yes, I know, and I am going to tell you. The right hon. gentleman-I will be charitable to him-displays his lack of knowledge. The Naval department will get these men, not from the schools, but from the fisheries of this country, from the men who are to-day engaged either in the fisheries or in the merchant marine, not, thank goodness, the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, which the leader of the Opposition is responsible for wasting $80,000,000 on, but the real merchant marine. These young men in the spring and summer will be engaged either in the off-shore fisheries, the -deep-sea fisheries or the shore fisheries of this country; they will be earning money and bringing wealth from the sea into this country. In the fall of the year, when they give up their vocation of fishing, if I understood the minister's programme correctly, they will be taken to the naval base at Halifax. I think the minister would be beter advised if he would have the men at Lunenburg where they are; but they will be taken to the city of Halifax and trained at the naval dockyard there where the greatest extravagance took place during the time when the leader of the Opposition was a member of what was known as the Union government. After they have been trained for ten or twelve days, if necessary they can be taken out on the high seas and trained either on mine sweepers or the two destroyers which the late Minister of Marine and Fisheries accepted from the British government. I think the idea is an excellent one, although I am not much in favour of a Canadian navy. In the first place, I do not think this country can afford a navy; but it can afford a certain amount of training for our fishermen and sailors, because after they have the training there is no necessity for them to go into the British navy or the Americain navy or any other navy; they can return to their vocations and help to pay the public debt of this country. They will go aboard the ships of the Canadian merchant marine, and they will be of some value to this country.
If the Minister of Defence brought in an estimate of $5,000,000, or $10,000,000, or $50,-000,000-and that would not give us half a decent navy-what would happen? We would have thousands of men taken from a productive industry and put into a non-productive industry, and we would try to make
Supply-Defence

ourselves believe that we had a Canadian navy. If we spent $5,000,000, could we defend our shores? The leader of the Oppposi-tion does not know anything about the matter; he does not know' whether it will take $10,000,000, $20,000,000, $50,000,000, or $100,000,000 to protect our Canadian shores properly. The leader of the Opposition, during the war, helped to vote $30,000,000 for what was called a navy to protect our Canadian shores, and we had to call on the United States government and the Japanese government to protect our Pacific and Atlantic coasts. That is the kind of naval policy my right hon. friend had; yet he dares criticise the present Minister of Defence for the volunteer naval reserve for which he asks in the small amount we are asked to supply to-night. It is amusing to me, almost as amusing as it was when the leader of the Opposition was talking about the strike at Glace Bay. He did not know a single, solitary thing about the matter; yet he dared get up and endeavour to make us believe that the county court judge had not the proper authority to call out troops. Of course, we do not mind the leader of the Opposition; he is a sort of joke on this side of the House.
The leader of the Opposition, of course, criticises this expenditure. What I would suggest to the Minister of Defence would be to clean up the mess in*the naval dockyard at Halifax, which mess is the result of the work of the government of the leader of the Opposition during the war and since the war, and of what was called the Purchasing Commission which was never authorized by parliament and which was appointed by the leader of the Opposition and his colleagues against the wish of parliament. They spent about $8,000,000 in buying stores which were not necessary; they put them into the naval storehouse at Halifax with the result that, to-day, after the Minister of Defence has sold some of the stores at about a quarter of their value, because he had to do so, there are still at the naval dockyards at Halifax about $2,000,000 worth of stores, and the leader of the Opposition more than anyone else in this House is to blame for that condition of affairs. Therefore, he should be the last one to talk in this House about extravagance or waste of money.
At the present time, due to the bungling of the late Union, National Liberal, Conservative, Tory Government, the people of this country had saddled upon them five ships. These ships were no good to the British navy and those gentlemen of the late Union government had those ships thrust on them. This present government had the good sense to lay up the
[Mr. Duff.l
big ship called the Aurora but at the present time they have two destroyers, the Patriot and the Patricia. Those ships are useless for naval purposes; but they can be utilized, and I am going to sugest to the minister to-night a way in which they can be used. Some time last Ostober, one of those boats was sent through the Panama canal and she is now on the Pacific coast. We have only two boats and the Pacific coast is entitled to one. Instead of bringing her back in the spring and spending a large amount of money in order to do so, I would suggest that the minister leave her on the Pacific coast. We have on the Atlantic, one known as the Patriot, and I would suggest that the minister put her to some practical use. This boat is no good for any purpose of defence; but we have a serious situation, not exactly on the Atlantic coast, but on the Atlantic ocean during the summer time. I am sorry the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) is not in his place, because this matter which I am going to discuss now, I am discussing as much for his benefit as for that of the Minister of Defence. Many fishing vesesls, carying some 3,000 men, proceed every year from Nova Scotia to the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, where they anchor and the men fish for about four months of the year. In addition to these Nova Scotia vessels which anchor on the banks and from which the men fish, there come over from France what are known and what the leader of the Opposition referred to as trawlers. I do not believe the leader of the Opposition knows what a trawler is any more than he knows what a mine sweeper is. A trawler is a fishing vessel which fishes with an otter-trawl. These come from France and they can fish off the Grand Banks as well as our Nova Scotia vessels. During the last two years these French vessels have committed great depredation to the fishing gear of the Nova Scotia vesesls, and it has been impossible for the fishermen of these Nova Scotia vessels to do anything to prevent the destruction of their gear. These French trawlers swoop down, sometimes in the day and sometimes at night, where the sailing vessels' gear is set and they destroy not only the gear itself but all the fish on it with the result that a great loss accrues to the fishing vessels of Nova Scotia. I would suggest to the minister that during the summer months when the fishing season is at its height the destroyer Patriot be sent to the Grand Banks of Newfoundland with the Nova Scotia fishing fleet. She will do more good there than she can going up and down the coast of Nova Scotia, and she would be able to afford protection to the fishermen.

Supply-Defence

We shall have to let her
off for the boat race.

I shall come to that in a moment. I say that this destroyer can do more work accompanying the fishing fleet than she can patrolling the Nova Scotia coast. If any depredation is committed the captain of the fishing vessel can notify the captain of the destroyer, who can ascertain the name of the French trawler and bring the matter to the attention of the Canadian authorities. I think that some international arrangement should be made with the French and the Canadian governments whereby something might be done to put a stop to these depredations.
The Minister of National Defence referred to the fact that one of these boats might be used in connection with the fishermen's races. I must thank this government on behalf not only of my own constituents but of the people of Nova Scotia generally for his generous act last fall in attaching the destroyer Patriot to the race and giving her up to the international race committee. This destroyer did good work while the preliminary races, were being-held off Halifax. The minister was good enough to send the Patriot to Gloucester with the racing vessel Bluenose. During the races in Gloucester the citizens of Nova Scotia were proud to see the Union Jack flying from the stern of the Patriot. She was only small, it is true, but she did represent Canada. I must also thank the government and especially the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for helping us in our time . of trouble during that race.	It may be
recalled by hon. members that a sad accident occurred at that time. One of the crew of the Bluenose accidentally fell into the dock and was drowned after the last race. The Prime Minister and the Minister o? National Defence, on leaminig this fact, immediately telegraphed to the captain of the Patriot, with the result that the body of the sailor was taken to his home town in Lunenburg on the destroyer. On behalf of my constituents, on behalf of the International Fishermen's Racing Committee, and on behalf of the people of the province of Nova Scotia I wish to take this occasion to thank the government for their action in this regard.
Now, I think that if the minister carries out the idea of a volunteer reserve it would be a good thing for Nova Scotia. In that way perhaps a number of young men who, if they had no naval reserve training, wight think of becoming second-rate lawyers, would with this training become good sailors, mates and captains and good citizens. I am willing
to give this volunteer naval reserve idea a fair trial, so that instead of having quibbling laywers we might have good citizens who would be able to help us in the production that is so much needed to-day.

I do not think the resolution should carry until adequate expression is given to the profound gratitude of the House for the inimitable manner in which the hon. member (Mr. Duff) not only sounds the depths of ignorance of all other members, but displays his own supreme erudition on every subject under the sun.

I did not say every member;
I said you, and you alone.
You are a burlesque.
I did not refer to anyone else.
It is an undying advantage to the House that we have among us one who can speak with pontifical authority on every subject from sewer gas to angels' wings.
You should be modest.

The non. member was moved by very deep and pathetic sympathy for me, ignorant as I was, not knowing even what was to become of these trained cadets after they had got the advantage of government, service at Esquimalt and Halifax. In his sympathy for me, and for the House in having to listen to me, he rose to tell us all about it. "Why," he said, "the member does not know where these boys are coming from. I will tell him where they are coming from; they are coming from the fishing vessels, from the fisheries, and they are going to be trained at Esquimalt and Halifax. They are not going to be trained for any purposes of a military or naval character. No, that would be a waste of their time." I hope the minister got that. "That would be a waste of their time. They are going to be trained [DOT] from ten to fourteen days and then are going back to fish, and they will be better fishermen as a result of the training the minister is going to give them on the trawlers."
Mine sweepers.

Yes. So at last we have the exalted purpose of Canadian Naval policy as now practised. It is to make better fishermen of those who are now suffering the depredations of French vessels on the shores of Nova Scotia. It is to teach the boys how to catch more fish from the water in order to feed the people of Canada. That is the purpose of the naval policy of the Minister of National Defence, according to
Supply-Defence

tliis court of appeal of last resort from the county of Lunenburg.
Well, I thought I was only stating a very simple truth and one generally accepted when I said-without the advantage of this later information-that this $1,500,000 was wasted, in so far as the defence of our country is concerned or in doing of the slightest thing to contribute to that defence, which others are now providing. When I stated that this money was wasted I thought I was uttering the simple truth. I felt fairly confident I was right. I must admit that for the moment I forgot that the same assertion was made a year ago by the hon. member for Lunenburg. Had I remembered that he was of the same opinion I should have had serious doubts as to the soundness of my view. But now that I utter again his conviction of a year ago he is lost in dismay at my ignorance.

I did not mention the word
"ignorance"; I said lack of knowledge.
That is more technical.

Let us leave the member for Lunenburg and come to the trawlers now christened the mine sweepers. Is the purpose of our naval policy really what the hon. member says it is? Are these vessels really to do what he says? Is the object of this training to send boys back to be better fishermen or to send them back to some mercantile marine, to be able, as I suppose, to handle the rigging of the mercantile ship a little better? Is the hon. member for Lunenburg rigt? Let us ascertain whether or not we have a naval service and whether we should vote a million and a half for what is actually being done to-day. That is what is before the committee for consideration. Do not let us deceive ourselves into thinking that we are lifting a hand by a burlesque of this sort to aid in that naval defence of which we share the advantage every hour. We are not. It would be far manlier of us to sweep the decks clear and say that we are not, and to stand before the world in our true colours. When we have a Minister of Defence who says we cannot go to the high seas because it would be too dangerous for the light craft that we have and that the high seas must be swept clear by someone else; when we have a Minister of Defence who is compelled to make such an admission, compelled by the exigencies of the policy of which he is sponsor, then we are doing nothing whatsoever in the way of defence, and it would be far manlier of us to say that we are doing nothing and to make the records of the House and the estimates show that we recognize the fact.

Now, it has been stated here that we met the last emergency without adequate provision ourselves. I know quite well we did. I know the necessity of adequate provision was scoffed in this House year after year. We were told that we were March hares and April fools because we ventured to suggest that something in the way of a manly effort should be made to provide against a contingency that seemed at least to be looming in the near future if not on the immediate horizon. We the Conservative party attempted to provide against that contingency, we attempted to bear some share that we thought befitted the strength of this country. We were stopped, we were not able to get the requisite legislation through. Then the war came upon us and we were without provision. We might of course have had something of the nature of what we have to-day under the Naval Service Act, but there was no possibility of getting anything under that act that would be of any use at all. There is no one knows that better than the minister who is now the Minister of National Defence. The only thing we could get was along the lines we sought to provide and were prevented by the Liberal majority in the Senate. [DOT] That is why we had to depend upon the strong arm of the British navy when war came-an arm to v'hich no ounce of muscle was added by this Dominion.
And here we are now. If we are not ready to do something in the way of naval cooperation that is at least worthy the strength of this, the greatest Dominion of the Empire, do [DOT] not let us play with the subject. Do not let us put a million and a half dollars in the estimates and tell the world in one breath and through the mouth of the responsible minister, "This is naval defence"; and then through the mouth of his parliamentary deputy, "This is merely to make better fishermen of our boys-a method of increasing the fish production on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts." I think we ought to stand forth in our true colours. I do not think this proposal is of any value. It must be plain that it is not. To be training for a life that our fishermen cannot follow in any naval vessels of ours is useless. If they intend to follow a naval career in another country, the place to be trained is there. To be trained for action on vessels that do not exist, and that the minister will not say are in contemplation to exist-well, surely that is nothing better than a sham.
Now, would ^t not be wisdom to wipe out the vote altogether rather than to go on in this way? Do not let anyone say that this is my policy. I think we ought to do something

Supply-Defence
worthy of this Dominion. I do not think we ought to expend on a naval service the equal per capita of what the Mother Country does. She has responsibilities that are not ours in an equal share. But we ought to do something that is worthy of our standing, of our strength, of our responsibility, of our wealth, of our exposure here on two coasts, worthy of our place in the Empire, the place we have won. I think the government would be well advised to come before parliament with a programme that measures up to these requirements.
Mr. DUFF. Before the vote carries, Mr. Chairman, I would explain for the benefit of the leader of the Opposition why it is wise to spend this money on the volunteer naval reserve. I think it is well known to most hon. members that the men who join the British navy do not come from the colleges or the schools of the Old Country; they come from the British fishing fleets and the mercantile marine. It is a well-known fact to every hon. member that when the war broke out thousands,-yes, tens of thousands of fishermen and merchant sailors were transferred to the navy and did invaluable service in the North Sea and other parts. Does not every one know that even in our own country men were taken from the fishing fleets on the Pacific and the Atlantic coast and from our merchant marine? They were the only men the government could get for naval duty during the war. They were the men that the government, of which the leader of the Opposition was a member, used on the leaky trawlers and old tug boat3 with which they pretended' to defend the shores of Nova Scotia. Is it not a well-known fact that the fishemen from the island of Newfoundland were perhaps, the very best men among those that took an active part in the operations of the British navy at Gallipoli? And yet the leader of the Opposition has the temerity to get up in this House and say that the Minister of Defence does not know what he is going to do with these men after he trains them. If war broke out tomorrow, and Great Britain needed more sailors for her navy, we could send thousands of men across the ocean for service in the North Sea or anywhere else. It is not necessary that these men should join a naval vessel after they complete their training in our fishing boats or in the mercantile marine. Their training during the rest of the year is probably just as effective as any training they will get under this scheme of the Minister of Defence.
The leader of the Opposition must have forgotten history when he criticized what the
Liberal party did for the naval defence of Canada. Why, if I were a Tory I would be ashamed to mention a word about our Canadian navy. Was it the Liberal party or the Tory party that brought down the Laurier Naval Bill? Was it not the Tory party which voted against that measure under which the Liberal party wanted to build ships for the defence of Canada? What did the Tory party do for naval defence? What naval vessels did we have to protect our coasts when war broke out? It is quite true that in 1912 the Tory government tried to vote $35,000,000 as a contribution to Great Britain for the building of three dreadnoughts, which would have been attached to the British navy in the North Sea. What use would they have been for the defence of Canada? And would they have been manned by Canadian boys? That was the naval policy of the Tory party in 1912. What happened in 1914 when war broke out? Had they spent one dollar for naval defence up to that time? No. Even the four ships that we provided under the Laurier administration were out of commission, due to the fact that certain Nationalists in the province of Quebec had the Tory party by the throat. Those vessels were tied up at the docks, the Niobe at Halifax and the Rainbow at Esquimalt. It took six weeks to put the Niobe in commission for war service. And'yet the leader of the Opposition dares to criticize the Liberal party and the Liberal government in regard to their record on naval defence. If our policy had been carried out in 1910, Canada would have had an effective navy when the war broke out. But because the Nationalist friends of the Tory party would not allow them to continue the Laurier naval policy we were left totally unprotected against attack by the German navy. I think it is high time the leader of the Opposition stopped talking about what the Tory party did for the naval defence of this country.

Before the resolution carries, Mr. Chairman, I must express my surprise at the developments which have taken place during recent years. It has generally been conceded that one of the most difficult positions to fill is that of an expert seaman on board a man-of-war, but apparently under the present system it is only necessary to teach men to be good fishermen and they automatically become good navy men. Nine days' training will equip an ordinary fisherman so that he will be equal to anything that may be required of him for the naval defence of this country.
I was also surprised at the references to the Canadian navy made by the hon. member
Supply-Defence

who preceded me (Mr. Duff) and what his party had attempted to do while in office previous to 1911. Notwithstanding the fact that they had occupied the .government benches for about sixteen years, during all that time not a contract was let for the building of a single warship. They went out of office and that was the condition of affairs that confronted their successors. It was well known that it would have been impossible to establish shipyards in this country and do anything effective in the way of building ships of war in the short period during which the administration that succeeded the Liberal government was in power. An attempt was made to vote $35,000,000 for the building of three dreadnoughts on the other side, where the work could be quickly done and there was reasonable prospect of rendering aid at a time when it was needed.

The hon. member says we
could not build warships in this country from 1911 to 1914, when the Conservative government was in power. Is it not a fact that under the Union government 63 ships were built from November 1918 to some time in 1920?

My hon. friend's
question is about as consistent as his argument tha^ fishermen are competent to man ships of war. No one would suggest that these poor little wooden ships of the mercantile marine were competent to defend the coasts of this country or to go out and meet the enemy. Who ever would take that view must be-well, I will not attempt to describe the condition his mind must be in.
The ships that the Union government built from 1918 on were not wooden ships; they were steel ships.

It was impossible to build shipyards here from which ships of war could be turned out that would be competent to meet the enemy-impossible, in any event, to turn them out in time. As late as June 1914, hon. gentlemen opposite were saying that no emergency existed, were pointing out that the sky was clear, that there were no clouds on the horizon, and that there was no need of taking any particular action in the matter of defence. It is also significant that even at that time the leader of the government, instead of taking notice of the criticisms that were being levelled against the administration, was organizing the various departments in order to be ready in the event of anything happening. The deputy ministers of the various departments and members of the Militia

Council were a committee organized for that purpose. My hon. friend says that the Liberal party had a policy; but the Liberal party went out of power without doing anything. It is true they called for tenders for the building of ships, but those tenders were filed away for months and no contract was let; nothing was done. Now we find the government asking the committee to pass an item of this size without any pretence that anything effective will result. They say it is merely to equip trawlers and mine-sweepers. I can scarcely understand the minister referring in a jocular way to these trawlers as mine-sweepers, when he knows perfectly well that there is no necessity for mine-sweepers at this time; they are being employed, as the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) has said, for fishing purposes. So we are voting this money for trawlers to go on the fishing banks of Newfoundland and elsewhere.
Not at all.

The hon. member
pointed out that one of these ships of the navy should be accompanying the fleet in its fishing operations off the banks of Newfoundland and also off the Pacific coast. It is the greatest burlesque ever brought before Parliament to ask the committee to vote money, supposedly for the naval service, but, according to one who claims to be an authority on the subject, actually for trawlers for fishing purposes.

I think the name "mind
sweeper" would be appropriate, because you would have to sweep your mind diligently to find a word that would give to what we have now in the way of vessels for the purpose of defence the dignity of a Canadian navy. I have nothing to say about the Conservative or the Liberal party so far as past policies are concerned. Mistakes may have been made. If the Liberal policy of 1910 had been put into effect, we might now have a navy which could be regarded as a real defence unit. At present, however, we have nothing. It is admitted on all sides that we need a certain amount of defence on the high seas. We have extensive coast lines on the east and on the west and whether we like it or not, these are to-day being protected by the Mother Country. We may not claim that they need protection, but it is a fact that we are producing largely for export trade; our mercantile vessels must sail the high seas, and if our markets are to be kept open in different parts of the world it is essential that these trade routes should be protected. We as a part of the empire should

assume our share of that burden of protection We are just as well able to bear the burden as Great Britain is, in fact, the people of Great Britain are more heavily taxed than we are. A nation canot live unto itself, and if we have arrived at the point where we can call ourselves a nation, we must bear part of its burden. We have entered into the League of Nations and that League has declared that in some way or other the whole world must be policed. Are we, as a self-governing nation within the empire, taking our part in national defence? If the policy advocated by the minister is a step to that end, I am willing to support it. But I sincerely hope that the policy advocated by the Liberal party twelve or thirteen years ago may one day be put into effect, so that we may be able to hold up our heads in the world, of which we are one of the important nations.
